Burrill Crohn

Burrill Crohn is a documentary filmmaker and owner of Jazz Images, Inc. His films include the five-part “History of Jazz” series, “Women in Jazz,” and a concert documentary, “Joe Williams/A Portrait in Song.” Burrill’s interests extend beyond the jazz world, and his current project is entitled “Playing with Parkinson’s,” about musician Sangeeta Michael Berardi facing the challenge of Parkinson’s disease.
Burrill was interviewed on January 3, 2012 in Woodstock, NY, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and I’m interviewing for the Jazz Archive at Hamilton College, in Woodstock. And I’m happy to have Burrill Crohn with me, who is usually on the other side of the camera.
I could still do it if you want.
You could do it. And we could get a cardboard cutout of you.
Well I could use my body double.

You know those terms. I just had to laugh at myself because we were doing an audio check and instead of going “check one two three four” you had all the other numbers. I don’t know if that’s from hearing “one two three four” too often.
Of course it is. It’s also the magic numbers. You know I just uttered a secret formula that allowed me to double myself so I could be behind the camera at the same time.
Could I have you repeat the little phrase you said when you got your Ace award, which you just told me about.
Sure.
I liked it.

So in 1987 I won an Ace award which is the cable equivalent of an Emmy. Back then they had Emmys for broadcast television, and the Ace for cable television. A couple of years later they merged and became the same thing, but it was the same thing. The crowded theater in Hollywood, the searchlights outside, tuxedos, you know. And so I won it as a writer for my “History of Jazz” series, before Ken Burns, and so what I said was — I practiced this — was that I thanked all the people you’re supposed to thank — David Chertok, the film collector, Wynton Marsalis, Chick Corea, Branford — good move Monk.
Sorry.
Should I keep going?
You want to start that story again? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Yeah. So real quick I’ll sum up. Back then the Ace awards were for cable and Emmys were for broadcast television, because they merged them. It was the same type of ceremony, broadcast on HBO. Searchlights, tuxedos, crowded theater everything. And I won it as a writer. And I was very nervous and I’d rehearsed an acceptance speech. And I got up in front of the crowd. The first thing I said is this is the wrong side of a camera for a writer to be on. But then I thanked all the people, David Chertok, the film collector, Branford Marsalis, Wynton Marsalis, Chick Corea and the people I work with. And then I said, “And I want to thank jazz itself, born in the U.S.A. a hundred years ago, and re- born every time someone takes a solo.”
Nicely said.
And deeply felt.
And you are player yourself?
Of sorts.
I actually haven’t introduced you on the film quite yet, for those people who will be watching us. Do you call yourself a documentary filmmaker?
I call myself a documentary filmmaker, yeah.
And you wear different hats as a writer.

Well I can do all the things involved with making a film. If I have enough money I don’t want to do any of them, I just hire people. But the way things have gone, these days you have to do everything almost.

I had this thought earlier today when we were with Warren Bernhardt, and then thinking about what you do and what he does, and a little bit of what I do, and that we sort of live on the fringe. But I think it’s important.
I don’t think Warren lives on the fringe. Warren is right in the center of existence.
Okay.

I mean as he says, he’s a blessed person, and everything he does seems to turn out right no matter what he does. I mean what he says, how he plays, where he’s been, the things that have just happened to him in life, it’s like this is a blessed existence. I’m sure he has his ups and downs like everybody else, but man, what a life.
Yeah. Born under the piano so to speak.
Born under the piano so to speak. So I don’t think Warren is on the fringe of anything. But the rest of us —
Well I have to wonder, I have asked musicians what led them to such an occupation, and I’ll ask you the same thing. Why do you do what you do?

Okay. You mentioned that I’m a player. I love to play when I play. I first became aware of the sound of the trumpet at the same time I became aware of sex. It was just about the same thing. It was Harry James and I was just like oh my God. And I used to dream, © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

daydream, that someone would give me a trumpet and I’d be able to pick it up and play it. And it didn’t turn out like that. And I went to college and the guy down the hall had a trumpet, and I used to listen to him practice, and when he left he gave me a mouthpiece and an Alban book, which is the classical book for studying. And I basically taught myself to play. I took my fingering out of the chart in the Alban book. Anyway but I always loved music. And I realized after a while that I was not good. I could play but I wasn’t that good. But the love of music never went away. And I listened to jazz and I’d go hear jazz, and, as Warren says, jazz touched my heart. And I listened to classical music, but it was jazz that touched my heart. So I actually began life, after a couple of false starts in different areas, as a writer. And I used to write educational materials. And gradually, as the medium for educational materials switched from print to multimedia, I started writing different multimedia forms, including films, for instance slide shows. And then when the first portapak video cameras came out in the early seventies, I picked up one of the first portapaks and I just go oh I want to do this. And somewhere along the line I got the dream of I want to make documentaries and I want to make documentaries about music, about jazz. And it was just a whole new vision — call it something from inside — I wanted to do this. And I didn’t know anything about filmmaking.
Was there a model for you? Things to look at?

No. I mean the more I started doing it the more I looked at other people’s work. But I’ll just finish, so I happened to know someone at what was then called ABC Video Enterprises, which was the forerunner of Arts & Entertainment Network. And I went to them — I think I contacted David Chertok, the film collector. I saw an article about him in the New York Times. And I went to him and I said, “David, let’s do a history of jazz series together.” It was very bold, I’d never made a film. Oh I take it back, I take it back. So I went to this guy and I said I wanted to do a history of jazz series. Come to think of it I had contacted David, and I even gave him, which was silly, a deposit, like an advance against some of the work so that he wouldn’t work with anybody else, he’d do this with me. And then I went to A&E, this guy I knew, and I said, “Let’s do a history of jazz series.” And he went to his bosses. And at this time, it was very interesting — A&E during the day broadcasts women’s programming — beauty shows, health shows. And at night they did cultural programs. So their bosses came back to me and said, “How about doing a women in jazz series?” And I knew a lot about jazz but I didn’t really know about women in jazz but I figured I’ll find out. So I said okay, I’ll do that. And that led to the first thing I did which was a series of “Women in Jazz” narrated by Marian McPartland for the instrumental side, and Carmen McRae for the vocal side. And that played for a long time. But I didn’t know what I was doing. I learned as I went along. Remember Billy Rigo? He came with me to the Joe Williams shoot? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
He was on board for that.

Billy — I showed him the clip of Wynton Marsalis, he was directing that shoot. And I remember saying, “Billy, what’s time code?” I didn’t even know what time code was when I started. But somehow I bluffed my way through and it came out okay. And I wrote them and I produced them and I directed them, and blah-blah-blah. So I just had this vision that this was what I wanted to do, and I learned as I went along.
How did it feel the first time you saw the scroll with your name on it.

It felt great. Warren was talking about his parents. My parents were not quite the same way. I remember I went down to where my parents were living at the time and I put on this station and I played this show. My parents never — my father would play classical music. He hated jazz. He hated my playing the trumpet jazz. And when — it was a half hour show I showed him and then the scrolls showed up, written and directed by Burrill Crohn. I was in my forties then. And he said, “Very nice. Too bad it took you so long to do it.” A knife into my heart.
Oh gee.
After that, the first time you see your name on television it’s a big thrill. After that it just comes routine.
Nowadays we can talk about jazz education, we can have the same conversation about film education. Do people need to go to film school?

You know these days, because people are so computer literate and so many programs make it easy to do anything, I think kids come out of grade school or out of secondary school, if they have any interest in video at all they can do digital editing, they’ve shot on cameras. I mean I think if you want to go make feature films there’s two reasons to go to film schools. You do learn a lot and you get a lot of hands-on experience, and you make great contacts. You work on other people’s films, they work on yours, and when the time comes when the people get a Hollywood contract they call their friends to work on the film. I never was good in school at anything. I always had to learn my own way.
Was your degree in writing?
Comparative literature — with a minor in psychology.
I like — you used the term “film strips” I can remember the beep — turn the dial.
Exactly. And after a while they became automated to the beep would activate the slide projector.
Not to get too off the track but it’s amazing how much technology has changed in a brief fifty years.

Astounding. I mean just — we were talking about looking up things on YouTube, just Google. I mean if you want to do any research you had to go to the library and go through the stacks, and now you just Google something and all this information comes up. I mean © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

that alone is an astounding revolution. I mean I used to have reference Encyclopedia Brittanicas and this book and dictionaries, and my desk was surrounded by them. Now I’m surrounded by hard drives and computers.
And what do you think of that?

Oh I think it’s 90 percent good and 10 percent I think bad, because I think the sense of scholarship is lost. I used to teach jazz history up at RPI. And I realized people can find things so easily, and they take what they find on YouTube or on the ‘net — the first thing that comes up is their primary source and they don’t dig any deeper. I mean you must run into that at Hamilton. And so they don’t get really immersed in the subject. It’s a little bit like some people say about the difference between working in video and film. In film you’ve got something concrete that you have your hands on, something, it’s a physical, tangible thing. Looking up stuff in the library and reading books is a physical — there’s something about the medium, there’s something tangible. I don’t know whether you take it in more. I’m not sure about all that. But I still prefer reading books than reading e- books. And it’s a little bit of the same thing. I love the ease of the computer. I can do things, edit on the computer, with a little 15, 17, 18 hundred dollar laptop and a program that now costs about three hundred dollars, that I was spending about three hundred dollars an hour to edit on back in the eighties. And that’s astounding. But you don’t have that intimacy.

Yeah. I think there’s something to be said for smelling the book mold in a library. And it’s very easy to sound old fashioned, like oh come on get with it. But the effort you have to make to go somewhere, and do the research, to me there’s value to it.

Well it’s a little bit like I remember going to a — I don’t gamble and I’m not interested in casinos, but I went to see a magician I knew play in Atlantic City at a casino. I forgot which one. And it’s a 24-hour environment. They have trees and they have waterfalls and things like that. And it’s like there’ll come a time in our life when that will be our environment and we’ll forget what a tree looks like, or smells like. And maybe not. Maybe things will change. I think the pendulum has swung too far and technology may be the ruination of us and the world may collapse in a certain way because of technology, and then the pendulum will swing back to whatever is left of earth and we will gain wisdom instead of intelligence and technology. Because what we gain in technology I think we lose in wisdom.
Wow. I’m glad that’s going to be written down. That’s a good statement.
Okay.
How about your experience hearing jazz live in clubs? Did it happen early on for you?
Yes. I mean as soon as I was old enough to get into a club, and even when I couldn’t. Yeah I was lucky. I grew up in New York. I was born in Paris but I moved when I was © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

very young, and there was jazz everywhere in New York back then. And my early taste was to swing, because the people I listened to were the big bands and Harry James. I remember finding an early recording of Harry James where he played a great recording. He played in a small group in Chicago. It was unbelievable, that small group stuff. And I remember going to 52nd Street and hearing Wilbur and Sidney DeParis. You know who they are. And then, but then I heard Roy Eldridge and I actually heard Bird before he died, just once in a little club, what was it called, I can’t remember. I know it was on the corner of Third and MacDougal — The Open Door. That’s what it’s called. And as I grew older I heard a lot of people. I heard Mingus and Monk. I heard Coltrane.
Can you recall, at the time, however old you were, were you aware that you were listening to legendary people?

Excellent question, excellent question. No I don’t think so, looking back. By the time I first heard Miles I knew he was legendary. I heard Miles at Café Bohemia. But by and large — and the other thing was you could go out and hear the legends but you could also go hear someone you never heard of play just as good and by whatever chance of fate or their own personality they never made it quote, the way the others did. I’ve talked to musicians who have stories who have traveled all over the country — they’ll go to a little club somewhere in a nowhere town and they hear a musician as great as anybody you’d ever hear. So there are a lot of geniuses out there that never saw the light of day. So I’m not sure how I felt. Because I grew up at a point where some of the people I heard were already becoming legendary like Monk and Mingus, so I was a little swayed by that. At the same time they were still young men. It’s sort of like a little bit of each.
At what point did you start going to live things and looking at them as a cameraman, or as a future documentary filmmaker.

Not until I started doing it I don’t think. I mean I really didn’t think that way until I suddenly got the urge. I did a film in 1981, it had nothing to do with jazz, it was called Anne Frank and Maine. A friend of mine was teaching the Holocaust at a little school with Gentile children in Maine, and he brought in the Holocaust as curriculum. And I thought that was just brilliant. And so I pitched the Anti-Defamation League and I got some money to go up there and make a film. And I didn’t shoot or anything at that time, I hired a crew. And I still remember the cameraman I hired and I saw him holding a camera and I saw him shooting, and I said I want to do that. And for the first time he let me hold a camera, oh it felt like so natural. But then he said, I just remember he said, “Shooting is one thing, but that’s the easy part. Lighting. That’s the art. Lighting is where the art comes in.” But I used to dream of having a camera. And then the first documentaries I did I did not shoot, I directed. And they had these beautiful cameras, these old Ikegami cameras. I mean they were seventy thousand dollar cameras. Beautiful © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

three chip cameras, we shot on one inch tape back then. But I just had a vision of myself having one of these and walking around the street. And one thing led to another and eventually — it was not that one but something like that. But it wasn’t until I started shooting on the portapak that I got a taste of doing that. But it wasn’t for a while until, actually the budgets changed and I had to learn how to do this myself.
Well it’s funny because when you said the cameraman said that it’s not the shooting it’s the — I thought you were going to say editing.

Well that’s true. And as any camera person will tell you if you know editing you’re already thinking about the editing when you’re shooting. But you know it’s interesting. I’m a classic ADD person. Oh God we’re going to go on a sideline here. Someone said that ADD was a useful trait before the Industrial Revolution, back when we were hunters and gatherers. Gatherers did repetitive tasks and they had to be aware in the future that if they planted their seeds and they knew their tasks in the spring would yield dividends in the fall. So they were like they were of the mentality of they could see into the future, they knew that repetitive tasks were good. The hunters had to be alert every moment, and went out in the forest, and the sound of a broken twig, or the movement, they had to be alert and ready to shoot. And I’m actually a fairly good cameraman, I think because — and also ADD people need to use their body and move around. They can’t be just in their head. Using their body grounds themselves. So when I’m with a camera I feel grounded. And I used to shoot rifles and I’m a good shot. I was very accurate as a marksman. And when you hold a camera and you move it, you feel one with the camera, you feel one with your environment, it’s like being a hunter. And one eye’s looking for what is coming up and the other eye is with the camera, and I feel more grounded, more alive, when I’m shooting as a cameraman than almost anything that I do. Because I’m using my brain and my body. I’m using my eye. I’m using all parts of my consciousness and my body and it’s where all the elements come together.
It sounds a little bit like jazz improvisation.

It is in a way and that’s a good point. I never made it as a musician but when you’re shooting you’re improvising all the time. And I also think that, as Warren would say, “Everything is everything. We’re all related.” Editing is also, you don’t create the piece, you wait for the piece to emerge and speak to you. What you’re editing. Rodin once said, “The sculpture is in the stone waiting to be revealed.” You don’t chip away and create something, it’s already in there. You just let it speak to you and you know where to chip. And out comes the sculpture that is already in there. And when I edit, if I don’t get too cerebral about it, I realize the film is in there. Now it’s footage, but somewhere the film is in there waiting to be — and you have to work really hard at clearing the debris around it to let it speak to you. And you go down many wrong paths too. You have to have a lot of © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

patience. I happen to be editing something now and I can’t do it on a part time thing. I have to clear away my life. I have to make sure there’s enough money that I don’t have to go out — because once you plunge into editing — it’s like writers talk about writing a book, they just plunge into writing a book. Joyce Carol Oates once said, “You don’t water the plants, you don’t dust your house, you don’t vacuum, you just write.”
Do you have to have a script to start a film?

No. Not at all. Au contraire. Well there are two types of documentaries. I take that back. The “History of Jazz” series I did we did have scripts. It was almost like the classical way of doing a documentary, you put index cards and one colored card is for the footage, the other colored card is for narration. And what we did before that, so much was based on the archival film clips we had, that the narration I wrote simply as a way to time together the clips. Like the clips were the gems on the tiara. [Ding] Ding. Fourth floor. Ladies’ Lingerie. The narration was the tiara which holds it. So in that case you basically follow the narration. But I don’t like to do a narration I like the film to create, in that case, no there is no script. And then you try to — the script emerges out of the video clips. They become a sequence in which the story is told.
Let’s talk about the logistics, the reality. Because earlier today we were talking about someone who wanted to make a film about Bill Frisell, and I remember I forget now, I wanted to write it down.

Let me put in a plug for her. Her name is Emma Franz, it’s F-R-A-N-Z, and she’s a jazz singer out of Australia, but she did this incredible film called “Intangible Assets Number 82” about an Australian drummer, Simon Baker, who was captivated by the sound of a Korean shaman. Shamans use drums to go into a trance. It was a shamanic drummer who is legendary. And he did many pilgrimages to try to see him and none of them ever quite worked. And she managed to go on one trip with a great crew, it’s a beautifully shot film. I’ll show you later. And she finally made the pilgrimage and met the drummer. And the shaman drummer died a couple of hours later — a couple of days later, not a couple of hours later. She is now doing a film on Bill Frisell.
And you said, I can’t remember the words, but you were referring to finding funding, like a hard nut.

You know I don’t know what they teach in film school because I didn’t go to film school, but the first thing they should do it teach us fundraising. I’m doing a film now that I think is going to be a wonderful film about a musician with Parkinson’s disease. The filmmaking is the easy part. The fundraising is the tough part. I have to stop and get something to drink.
I have a bottle of water actually. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Oh, if you could give me the bottle of water. Thank you so much. Are you putting on the headphone every now and then just to see whether the sound — you should see whether it still sounds good. My voice is getting raspy.
I’m hearing me.
No now you should hear me, how does that sound?
Yeah, sounds good.

Good. That was good to check. Here’s another little thing. In film school everyone teaches how to make video film and sometimes kids go away thinking that’s all there is. If you don’t get good sound, you’re screwed. Good sound can rescue bad video. You can never rescue bad sound.

I understand what you’re saying. And I noticed that, even in commercials or sometimes TV shows and you can tell when things have been vocally overdubbed. And sometimes I wonder, why do they have to do that?
Probably they didn’t have good sound.
Right.

But if you get good authentic sound, you can get the worse picture, but if the sound is good it’ll save — it won’t totally compensate, but you can get a lot of compensation if you’ve got good sound. But if you don’t have good sound I don’t care how good the picture is, people won’t want to hear that.
Well getting back to this, it’s almost step one, you get this idea and then you have to find some funding. Now you’ve got to research, right?

Well things have changed. Everything’s changing. Like technology is changing, information is changing, everything is changing. When I first started doing films, first of all budgets were bigger, because the price of entry was much more expensive. You are shooting on a camera that costs about three thousand dollars, if my memory serves me. I was shooting on cameras that cost seventy thousand dollars. Editing was three or four hundred dollars an hour, or you could edit off-line for fifty or seventy dollars an hour. But you have to go back to 1980s prices, which was double that today. And now you can edit on laptops, so everything is changing. Secondly, so therefore, if you could find sponsors, when I started doing the “Women in Jazz” I went to A&E and A&E paid for stuff. They paid for me, they ended up owning the footage, but I got paid for what I did. When I got the idea — no I didn’t get the idea, Leslie Gourse got the idea — but for those who are watching, I did a film on Joe Williams, a documentary on Joe Williams that Monk was very involved in and it actually came to me, but that was paid for by Hamilton College. And when I did the “History of Jazz” series I went to Japan. I spent a week in Japan negotiating a contract with what was then — it was the Japanese back then, they had money, and they were great jazz lovers. And they couldn’t wait to do © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

something about jazz. It was a big contract. It was like a half a million dollar contract to do a ten episode series on the history of jazz. David Chertok had set that up actually. And I spent a week in Japan with an attorney, sitting at a conference table with the Japanese. That was funny in itself because they had a translator there, and they would say something in Japanese and then translate it, and then we’d talk among ourselves, and then come up with our answer. And they would translate back to me. After a couple of days we realized they knew English as good as we did, but they were listening to what we were saying. But anyway, today like everything else is changing and like even Occupy Wall Street and Arab Spring and all that, that’s breaking down the hierarchy and everything is going more vertical. We’re turning to each other. Kickstarter — you know about Kickstarter?
Yeah.

Well Kickstarter, you look at all the stuff that’s being funded on Kickstarter, that’s people turning to each other for money. And I am doing this film — I need a lot more than what I’ve raised — but I raised eleven thousand dollars on Kickstarter, that helped me do a critical recording session with Sangeeta — the musician with Parkinson’s — and able- bodied musicians that he used to play with — a very critical part of the film. But I’m struggling now. I go to people, I ask people for money. I’ve gotten shameless. I mean what I really want is to have a producer come in and handle this part for me. But that’s hard to find, especially on a film like this that’ll probably not make a lot of money if it even makes its own money back. So I have to ask everyone for money, and do you need a tax write-off?
It’s like Warren was saying about that next step up of being a band leader.
Exactly. Exactly. He never wanted to do it. Exactly.
Smart.

You know I find I’m happier working with other people and okay, Burrill you do this part and you’ll do that part, rather than where I have to do everything myself. And I’m — hey, look at me, I’m not young anymore. And it gets hard.
Do you find that it behooves you to be aware of what you have to pay for — licensing and royalties and all that.

Oh sure. Oh sure. And you know even though I’m not terribly organized, I have spreadsheet programs where I put all the — some of it you have to guess at — but sure, when you raise money that’s part of what you raise money for. You have the whole overhead thing. You need an accountant. You need an attorney to advise you. You need someone to look over the releases and see if they’re okay, and then the music clearances, which — as you and I both know very well — we did this documentary on Joe Williams and there was enough money to pay for the documentary, and I say immodestly it’s very © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

good, because I just got out of the way and let Joe be himself. But it will never be seen on television unless we raise another fifty grand or so to clear all the music licenses and pay the Basie orchestra what they get — scale for television, which is a different thing from playing in a concert hall. And all this extra money has to be raised. So yeah.
Yeah, Jean Bach, “A Great Day in Harlem.”
Oh I know Jean, I know her editor, Sue Peehl very well.
Yeah. She said, “Yeah, go ahead and make your film, just don’t put any music in it.”
That’s right. That’s right. Make your film and don’t put any music in it, that’s exactly right. Or make your film and hire a composer to write the music.
Oh, yeah. Do you think people get the wrong idea, like oh you’re making a film, you’re going to make a lot of money on your film — I said a joke didn’t I?

Well yes and no. First of all, there are exceptions to every rule. And you know I’m crying poor here, but there was a period in my life when I did the “History of Jazz” series, there was a market for jazz films. And I had what they call a syndicator in England. He had a company called TCB, meaning taking care of business. His name was Angus Trowbridge — it’s a great British name — but he was an American and he lived outside of London. And he would go around to Cannes and different names of film festivals where buyers come, TV sent representatives and they come, and they buy. So he would only have jazz films. That’s what TCB was about. And he had these whole bunch of jazz films and he’d sell a package: okay you have two of Burrill’s films and three of this film and three of that film, and you’d buy the whole package. And then he would sell it, he’d take twenty- five percent for himself, and he’d send checks. And they would come in the mail. That was great. So I got paid for doing the film, and then we got paid afterwards. So nowadays — and of course there are always people like Ken Burns — Ken Burns makes money when he does — he makes money whatever he does. And I also mentioned, when you first contacted me, about being the first person, as a jazz filmmaker, I said I’m not the first person you should be interviewing. The first one is Bruce Ricker, who did “Last of the Blue Devils” and then he went on to become friends with Clint Eastwood. He did “Straight, No Chaser,” and he did a wonderful film on Louie Prima, and he did one on Harold Arlen and he did some beautiful films, and he made money from doing them. And then there’s Don McGlynn who’s probably the most prolific jazz filmmaker, “Mingus” and — oh I take it back, I take it back — it’s Don McGlynn who did Louie Prima and Harold Arlen and Mingus and Horace Parlan and Howlin’ Wolf. But Bruce did a couple of American Masters — he did one on Tony Bennett, that’s what he did, a really good film on Tony Bennett. So Don McGlynn and Bruce Ricker both did okay in jazz, and Don is very much alive and very prolific and still making films. He is a very good person to go talk to. And Don is a true film buff. He can talk about films for hours. He’s very © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

In that film, and in other places, when I read about jazz, I sometimes object to the idea that changes in music, jazz especially, are often because of social issues. To me they leave out the thing about people just experiment because they can, and because it feels good to do something new, or — Evan Christopher, who’s a clarinetist we’ve had at the college, had this interesting theory about why vibrato with the early New Orleans clarinetists, and it had to do with playing with out of tune pianos. You know, that kind.
Wait a minute. There’s vibrato and there’s vibrato. You have the vibrato of the clarinetist and then you have Sidney Bechet, which brought vibrato to a whole other level. He made vibrato an art form.
Right. He surely did.
I’m not sure I agree with that. I think that — did you ever read a book called — we were talking about this, how both of us are losing things — Jazz: A People’s Music?
I think I did. LeRoi Jones?

No, no, no, no, no. It’s a Marxist historian. It’s a very interesting book. It’s about music and social change and I found it a fascinating book when I read it. And I also think that if you look at the arts, I think everything is interconnected. I think that World War II, there was an innocence pre-World War II. World War II came, with the advent of the bomb, and with a sense all of us made for the first time that we could face extinction. That gave rise to a different form of literature, the existentialist writings and I think music changed also. There’s another thing, I really believe this, look at Bird and Dizzy, who were just phenomenal technicians. Now these are musicians who might have tried out for symphony orchestras but — would have wanted to try out for symphony orchestras but they never would get a chance. So whether it was conscious or unconscious, they developed their chops to an unbelievable degree. And then they had these cutting sessions and they’d take tempos at 320 or something like that, and say, “Okay white boy, come in and try to — you think you’re such good players, try to play this.” So whether that’s a conscious force or any unconscious force — or take what happened in World War I, when the 369th regiment band, James Reese Europe’s marching band came and they went to Europe, and they played in France, and they swung. And the French people responded, © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

partially because France was a colonial power. And they had a percent of African music in their DNA almost, let alone within their culture. So they saw black musicians as a carrier of a tradition from Africa, whereas America looked at black musicians as, what was jazz, this was like a sexual act. It was like lowbrow music. It was — oh it doesn’t qualify — all the rants against jazz will deprave you, it’ll make your children depraved, and all that stuff. But in France they recognized this music as an offshoot to African music. And the black musicians — women threw themselves at them, people brought them drinks, and a lot of them stayed after the war was over, in Paris and in France in general and in Europe, and they invited their friends to come over. And then the first jazz criticism was written by Frenchmen. And they helped Americans appreciate their own art form. So I don’t think musical development or any art form — there were people in the Vanguard who were ahead of the curve — like Bird was or Coltrane — but some of that’s spiritual. I think they’re in touch with the spiritual. You know you listen to a lot of musicians, and writers say this too and painters, some of they say, “It’s not me that’s doing the playing, this is something that passes through me.” I tune my own instrument, my body, my technique, just like you make a radio as pure as you can to receive transmissions that come through it. You make your own instrument as pure as you can so what comes through from some other planet or wherever music comes from, passes through you. It’s amazing how many quote famous musicians would say it’s not me playing, I’m just passing it on. So I think it’s all connected — history and social movements and spiritual stuff, and there are so many factors that come into play. I’m doing this film on this musician with Parkinson’s. I mean he lives in California but he happened to be here because he used to live here and he was visiting. film about this guy. So here I am. I don’t know how I’m doing it and whether I can raise enough money to finish it — I will.

on television, has been about music. And there is something about — I don’t think I’m a great filmmaker at all. I mean there are people with way better technical chops than me. Do you think it gets harder and harder to innovate in the world of jazz?

That’s a good question. Wynton talks about that. Keith Jarrett talks about that. But I still — Joe Williams said this wonderful thing in the interview, he said first you imitate, then you assimilate, then you innovate. And Warren talked about that. He said, you know, I’m not sure I was an innovator. And I even heard a panel discussion at the Institute of Jazz Studies about, like Clifford was a great player, a great player. But he wasn’t an innovator. The innovators are few and far between. They change the sound of the music. Miles was an innovator. Dizzy was an innovator. Dizzy changed — Louis was an innovator. He was the first one, obviously, unless you want to count Jelly Roll Morton. And then Dizzy came along and he changed all that, and then Miles changed all that, going from high technique to space and beautiful stretched out playing the way Jaki Byard was talking about. And then you know, Ornette changed the music. And I think also the other thing that you have to look at is that the classifications of music are breaking down.
Um hum. Like world music and everything.

Yeah. Which Karl Berger started at the Creative Music Studio. It’s improvised music, and it’s not improvised music. It’s a combination, a re-combination of things. So yeah, I think there are innovators all the time. There may be innovators that just remind you that music is not high — that bring you back to your heart for instance. There can be one guy out there who just plays — you hear something on — I used to play in this big band and there was this kid there at the time, a trumpet player named Gregg Glassman. And I began to listen to him playing and he had no technique at first. Now he’s got a lot of chops. But every solo he made came from the heart. It was like a poem coming out. And all these great trumpet players [scats] every note he played you could tell he was trying to make poetry. So there may be innovators out there that you never heard of. But if they remind you to come from your heart and not from your head, that’s an innovator. And yes, the innovators, hey, the first person who came out with electronics in music, like Jay Clayton uses voice doublers and changes of voice and unchained this pure voice and she started — so there are ways to innovate — I don’t see clear demarcations. Some people do something for the first time and people pick up on it. It becomes part of the vocabulary. A word that no one heard before after a while becomes part of the vocabulary.

I’ll tell you an incredible dream I had once and I don’t know if this makes it on camera or not. I once dreamt, this was a while back, that I was on this other plane of existence, and it was like a plane. It was just white everywhere. In the middle of this white was a piano, it was a Rosewood piano, it was gorgeous, and an old ancient scroll that — you know like these scrolls that you turn up for the piano? And on it was an illuminated manuscript, like the old illuminated manuscripts, the Medieval ones? And it had one page of music, just one staff. And on the staff, in the old Medieval writing with the square notes, it had the most basic triad — C-E-G. But the book was a hologram. And if you looked in it you could see the mysteries of the universe. And it was clear to me that if you sat down and played that triad with the right touch, the mysteries would be revealed. So I sat down at the piano. And as I sat down these entities, like spiritual beings in monk’s robes, and they didn’t walk, they glided over. And what I noticed is there was curiosity but not anticipation. There was not motion connected to it, they just wanted to see what I could do. And I sat down and I played the triad, even for me easy to play, but nothing happened. And they glided away, no disappointment. And even before I woke up I knew what the meaning of the dream was. I’ve been privileged enough to get into the playing of masters, because I’ve worked with a lot of well-known musicians in the course of what I’ve done, and met many, many more. So I got to their plane, but I was a long way to becoming a master. And what did it take to become a master? Just what it takes to play, I had to practice. Like Warren talks about practicing. It’s not playing the notes. He had this beautiful thing about getting to the heart of the note and the intent of the music, finding the intent. That’s what the dream was. That practice was not to get to the level of master, the next level was to go deeper and deeper and deeper, and that comes from practicing. And it’s interesting that you used the word, because practice applies to musical practice, and it applies to spiritual practice. It’s all connected.
